title: Dynamic arrays (newly learned)
summary: FILTER, UNIQUE, SORT and spilled ranges, with a safe fallback for older Excel.

lessons.title: Dynamic arrays: UNIQUE, SORT and FILTER (newly learned)
lessons.body:
Dynamic array functions return several values from one formula, and the result **spills** into the cells below and to the right. This is a skill you are learning now, not one from your job, so practise it next to the older tools.

**Availability.** Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and later, and Excel for the web have them. Excel 2019 and earlier do not, and a shared file shows `#NAME?`. If you do not know the version, a pivot table or Remove Duplicates is the safe route.

```text
=UNIQUE(array)                          distinct values
=SORT(array, [sort_index], [order])     order 1 ascending, -1 descending
=FILTER(array, include, [if_empty])     rows that meet a condition
```

Using the practice shifts loaded as `tblShifts` (id, pharmacy_id, pharmacist_id, requested_at, filled_at, starts_at, status, cancel_reason, is_emergency):

```text
=UNIQUE(tblShifts[cancel_reason])
```

This spills four rows: the three reasons and a blank. A blank source cell comes back as **0**, a classic surprise, so filter blanks out first when it matters.

```text
=FILTER(tblShifts, tblShifts[status]="cancelled", "None")
```

returns every column of the 171 cancelled shifts. Combine conditions by multiplying for AND and adding for OR:

```text
=FILTER(tblShifts, (tblShifts[status]="cancelled")*(tblShifts[is_emergency]=1), "None")
```

That returns the 33 cancelled emergency shifts. The third argument is shown when nothing matches, which avoids `#CALC!`. Nest them to build a ready report, newest first (requested_at is column 4):

```text
=SORT(FILTER(tblShifts, tblShifts[status]="cancelled"), 4, -1)
```

**Spill rules.** Type the formula only in the top-left cell. Refer to the whole result with the spill operator, for example `A2#`. If cells in the way contain data, you get `#SPILL!`; clear them. You cannot put a spilling formula inside a regular Table, so put it on the sheet beside the Table. Count rows with `=ROWS(FILTER(...))`, and the number of distinct pharmacies with shifts is `=COUNTA(UNIQUE(tblShifts[pharmacy_id]))`, which is 40.
keyPoints: UNIQUE, SORT and FILTER return many values that spill from one cell.
Multiply conditions for AND, add them for OR inside FILTER.
Blank source cells come back as 0; the if_empty argument avoids #CALC!.
#SPILL! means something blocks the result; not available in Excel 2019 or earlier.
lessons.interviewAngle: Say it plainly: "I have been learning dynamic arrays like FILTER and UNIQUE on my own; at work I got the same lists with filters and pivot tables." Know the version limit and offer a pivot or Remove Duplicates as the fallback. Do not claim long experience.

choices: All columns for each cancelled shift, spilling down, or "None" if there are no matches
A single count of cancelled shifts
Only the status column of cancelled shifts, without spilling
The cancelled shifts hidden inside the Table with a filter button
exercises.explanation: FILTER returns whole matching rows from the array and spills; the third argument is the empty-result message.

exercises.prompt: Inside FILTER, which operator combines two conditions with AND? (One symbol.)
exercises.explanation: Each condition is an array of TRUE/FALSE; multiplying gives 1 only where both are true.

exercises.prompt: Write one formula that lists the cancelled emergency shifts newest request first, and say how many rows you expect from the practice data.
exercises.answer:
```text
=SORT(FILTER(tblShifts,(tblShifts[status]="cancelled")*(tblShifts[is_emergency]=1),"None"),4,-1)
```
Expect 33 rows. Column 4 is requested_at and -1 sorts descending. It needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+; otherwise filter the Table by hand.
rubric: Wraps FILTER inside SORT with a column number and -1

lessons.title: Summaries with spilled ranges and a safe fallback
lessons.body:
Spilled results can feed other formulas, which lets you build a summary that resizes itself. Load `tickets.csv` (734 rows) as `tblTickets` and put this on a new sheet:

```text
A2: =SORT(UNIQUE(tblTickets[category]))
B2: =COUNTIFS(tblTickets[category], A2#)
C2: =B2# / SUM(B2#)
```

`A2` spills the five categories in alphabetical order. `A2#` means "the whole spilled range", so `B2` returns one count per category and spills beside it. `C2` turns the counts into shares:

| Category | Tickets | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Access | 123 | 16.8% |
| Bug | 184 | 25.1% |
| Data fix | 100 | 13.6% |
| Feature request | 122 | 16.6% |
| How do I | 205 | 27.9% |

The counts add to 734, which is your check against `=ROWS(tblTickets[id])`. If a sixth category appears in next month's data, all three formulas grow by themselves, which a hand-built table would not.

**Looking up with arrays.** `XLOOKUP` can return a whole row: `=XLOOKUP(20001, tblTickets[id], tblTickets)` spills the entire record for ticket 20001. `SORTBY(array, by_array, -1)` sorts by a column that you do not want to display. `SUM(FILTER(...))` replaces a SUMIFS when the condition is awkward.

**Wrap-up habits**

- Put each spilling formula where nothing sits below or to the right of it.
- Format the spilled range with the `#` reference so new rows inherit it, for example in a chart series or a data validation list (`=A2#`).
- Reconcile the total after building any summary.

**The safe fallback.** If the file may be opened in Excel 2019 or in a tool without these functions, build the same table with a pivot table: Category in Rows, Count of id in Values, Show Values As % of Column Total. It gives the same 205 and 27.9% for How do I, and it works everywhere. State which route you chose and why in your notes.
keyPoints: A2# refers to a whole spilled range, so dependent formulas resize with it.
SORT(UNIQUE()) plus COUNTIFS builds a self-growing summary.
Check that the counts add to the total (734 tickets).
A pivot table is the version-safe fallback.
lessons.interviewAngle: If a test lets you pick the tool, say why: dynamic arrays are fast for a live list, a pivot is safest for sharing. That shows judgement. Keep the honest line that dynamic arrays are newly learned and that pivots are your strong tool.

exercises.prompt: A2 holds `=SORT(UNIQUE(tblTickets[category]))` and spills five rows. What does `=COUNTIFS(tblTickets[category], A2#)` in B2 do?
choices: Returns five counts, one per category, spilling beside the list
Returns only the count for the first category
Returns a #VALUE! error because A2# is not a single value
Returns the total number of tickets five times
exercises.explanation: COUNTIFS accepts an array of criteria and returns an array of results.

exercises.prompt: Which operator refers to the entire spilled range that starts in A2?
exercises.explanation: The # after a cell address means its whole spill range.

exercises.prompt: Build the ticket category summary with counts and shares, say what total you must see, and give a fallback for Excel 2019.
exercises.answer: A2 `=SORT(UNIQUE(tblTickets[category]))`, B2 `=COUNTIFS(tblTickets[category],A2#)`, C2 `=B2#/SUM(B2#)`. The counts must total 734 (Access 123, Bug 184, Data fix 100, Feature request 122, How do I 205). Fallback for Excel 2019: a pivot table with Category in Rows, Count of id in Values and Show Values As % of Column Total.
rubric: Uses UNIQUE/SORT then COUNTIFS with the # operator
